title: Three-Way Heteronyms: 10 Words with Triple Meanings
description: Most heteronyms come in pairs, but a few words create three-way puzzles. Explore rare triple readings, near-triples, and how context reveals the right pronunciation.

content.text: Three-Way Heteronyms: 10 Words with Triple Meanings

Most heteronyms arrive in pairs: lead can guide a team or describe a grey metal, while wind can move through the trees or twist around a spool. But what happens when one spelling opens three doors? These three-way words are among English's best pronunciation puzzles. They are rare, and the definition needs care: a strict triple heteronym has three distinct words, meanings, and pronunciations. More commonly, one spelling has two pronunciations but three or more meanings. Both kinds are useful tests of how much context does for a reader.
What Counts as a Three-Way Heteronym?

A heteronym is a homograph — a word with the same spelling — whose meanings are paired with different pronunciations. A word such as bark does not qualify: dog bark, tree bark, and a boat's bark are different meanings, but they are pronounced alike. That is a homonym or a polyseme, not a three-way heteronym. The examples below therefore separate genuine pronunciation changes from near-triples: words that have two sound patterns and three useful readings.

rows: To guide; to be in first place; the metal element.
Moving air; to twist or coil; to turn a mechanism or bring something to an end.
Nearby; to shut; to finish or conclude.
A written account; the best achievement; to capture sound or video.
Here now; a gift; to show or deliver information.
A physical thing; an aim; to protest or disagree.
A planned piece of work; to cast or display; to estimate a future result.
Farm goods; to make; to bring something about or present it.
Waste material; to decline; to reject an offer or request.
What something contains; the material in a publication; satisfied.

content.text: The Rare Cases: When Three Sounds Really Appear

English dictionaries usually describe triple heteronyms as extremely uncommon. One reason is that pronunciation changes tend to create a pair, especially the familiar noun-versus-verb stress shift. A third pronunciation often belongs to a regional accent, an older use, a proper name, or a specialised word. That does not make the puzzle less interesting; it means we should label the third route honestly rather than pretend every extra sense is a new heteronym.

items.definition: This is a famous edge case. Depending on meaning and dialect, it can be pronounced like “sloo” for a marshy channel, “sluff” for shedding skin or getting rid of something, and with a further regional pronunciation recorded in some wordplay references. Check a dictionary before treating the third sound as standard in your variety of English.

The pronunciation varies between an adjective meaning able to move, a hanging sculpture, and the British noun for a mobile phone. The three-way effect comes partly from vocabulary and partly from regional English, so it is a useful reminder that accent can change a puzzle's answer.

In ordinary English, sin is a moral wrong. Capitalised Sin can refer to the Sumerian moon god, while Sin is also the name of an Arabic letter. These meanings do not all produce three sounds, but they show why spelling, capitalisation, and pronunciation must be considered separately.

Does can be the verb meaning performs, pronounced “duz”, or the plural of doe, pronounced “dohz”. It is a near-triple rather than a strict three-way heteronym, but it is a particularly effective context test because the written form gives almost no help.

content.text: When you meet a three-way candidate in writing, do not guess the pronunciation from the letters alone. First identify the word's grammatical job. An article often signals a noun — “a record” — while “to record” signals a verb. Then read the words around it: “the close window” means nearby, but “close the window” means shut. Finally, use the subject matter. A sentence about batteries may point to lead metal; a sentence about a captain may point to lead as a verb.

items.definition: Articles, infinitives, plural endings, and sentence position often reveal whether the word is acting as a noun, verb, or adjective.
The nearby words usually supply enough meaning to choose between the possible pronunciations. Is the object a thing, an aim, or a disagreement?
Many noun-and-verb heteronyms move stress: RE-cord becomes re-CORD, and PRO-ject becomes pro-JECT. The spelling stays still while the rhythm changes.
A pronunciation that sounds natural in Britain may sound unusual in the United States, and vice versa. Mark accent-dependent examples instead of calling one speaker wrong.

content.text: Why Three-Way Words Make Excellent Puzzles

A normal definition question has one obvious route from clue to answer. A three-way heteronym adds a second challenge: even after you recognise the spelling, you still have to select the right sound and meaning. That makes words such as lead, close, and record satisfying daily-puzzle answers. They reward vocabulary, sentence awareness, and a willingness to say a familiar word in an unfamiliar way.

The best strategy is to learn each reading inside a sentence rather than as an isolated list. Say “the record is clear” and “record the interview” aloud. Then make your own third sentence: “She broke the record.” Repeated context turns a surprising pronunciation into a reliable instinct — exactly the skill a heteronym puzzle exercises.
